title: Where do poison dart frogs get their poison?
hook: Raised in captivity, these bright frogs lose their poison.
summary: From their food: poison dart frogs store toxins from the small arthropods they eat; raised on crickets, they aren’t poisonous.

cardBlocks.text: The bright colours of poison dart frogs are a warning: they are among the most toxic animals on Earth. But the frogs don’t make the poison themselves. They store alkaloids, toxic compounds, by eating small arthropods and insects such as ants and mites, which most likely get the toxins from the plants they feed on.

Captivity is the proof. At the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in the United States, the frogs eat crickets, beetles and fruit flies, insects with no poison, so they are not poisonous. Scientists tested two ideas, that the frogs make the toxins or that they get them from their diet, and the diet explanation won.
Poison dart frogs get their poison from their food; raised on toxin-free insects, they aren’t poisonous.

deepDiveBlocks.text: In the brightest species, toxicity comes from a diet of ants, mites and termites. Species that eat a much wider range of prey tend to have dull colours and little or no toxicity.
The name comes from Indigenous South Americans using their secretions to poison the tips of blowgun darts. But out of more than 170 species, only four are documented as used this way.

heroMedia.alt: Diagram comparing two diets: in the wild, toxins pass from plants to ants and mites and on to the frog, which becomes poisonous; in captivity, fed toxin-free flies and crickets, the frog has no poison.
